utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And I notice Mr. Naletilic is absent. Is he still in illness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes. He is in the Detention Unit. He is still unwell, but we can continue without him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. Could we have the witness, please. Madam Usher, would you please bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shalom, my respects to all of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down. Yes, Mr. Seric. Your re-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Mandelbaum.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandelbaum, undoubtedly, as we heard yesterday, you're a man of huge experience, especially that acquired during the war, and a man who no doubt made an immense humanitarian contribution for the sake and benefit of all, of people of all faith and ethnic groups in Mostar, and I am sure that you could tell us a great deal, much more than the testimony here could allow it, to tell us about your life experience in Mostar and outside. But now, I would nevertheless ask you to try to listen carefully to my questions, to try to be as concise as possible, in order to avoid any misunderstanding and to have it recorded in the transcript as precisely as possible. So wait for me to finish. I'll make a sign when I've done so and then you can begin your answer. Mr. Mandelbaum, can you tell this Court, and all of us, with regard to the permits to leave the town, I mean the town of Mostar, who is it that you went to? Give us, please, only the names. And by this I mean the time between -- from 9th of May, 1993 onward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Poriouvaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. It is not stemming from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric. I don't think this question was asked in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that is not true. Mr. Poriouvaev examined the witness about the facts concerning his humanitarian activity, crossings from the east to the west side of the town, he examined him about the methods, and all these things. Yesterday a certain confusion in the transcript occurred. Many names are incorrect and were not recorded. I am not repeating my question from the direct examination; I'm merely following up on my learned friend's question, and I insist on it. Only names. But please give them slowly and precisely, and I want the witness to follow the transcript and to spell out all those names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes. [Microphone not activated] ... testimony of the witness we missed certain names in the transcript. In this sense, Mr. Seric, you are allowed to ask this question, but only limited to those names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is what I had in mind, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: So let me repeat the question. For the permits to leave the town, give us their names of people that you went to.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Berislav Pusic, called Berko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Just go -- take it easy and follow it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Head of the department for the exchange of prisoners and detainees. Mr. Slobodan Bozic, head of the department for cooperation with UNPROFOR and international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perica -- Mr. Perica Jukic, Minister of Defence of Herceg-Bosna. In his presence, General -- General Ante Roso was always with him. These are people on the Croat side. As for the Bosniak side, the permits were issued by Mr. Rusmir Cisic, Mr. Smail Klaric, Mr. Orucevic, orally. These are the people who were in charge of these permits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My next question, Mr. Mandelbaum, is: When you visited the Heliodrom, did you -- or rather, whom would you approach to gain entrance? Again, full names, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I went into the Heliodrom with Mr. Petar Pehar, Perisa. He is from Citluk - I do not know what office he held - with a view to exchanging a Bosniak who was at the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know any other name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. At the Heliodrom, after that, I entered the Heliodrom by going to the gate and introducing myself to the guards, and they would let me in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Next question. I know that you often help detained Muslims to leave the Heliodrom, which Vinko Martinovic couldn't do. Who is it that you went to at that time to get those prisoners released? Will you tell this Court: Whom did you speak to? I'm talking about May and June 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Poriouvaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has gone beyond the first question allowed by you, I would suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric. You have to limit your question within the framework of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the reason is -- for my question is the same, what Mr. Poriouvaev asked questions about. Admission into the Heliodrom and the precious humanitarian work of Mr. Mandelbaum during those sad events in Mostar. The question about his humanitarian activity, release of some Muslims. That is, all I want to know is the name of the person whom the witness approached to obtain the release of these detainees, and if that does not arise from the Prosecutor's questions, then I do not know what does. Only the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that this matter was not mentioned in the cross-examinations. Mr. Seric, if you missed that portion in your direct examination, I could allow you to ask this question again, on the condition that the Prosecution has the opportunity to cross-exam this witness on this point again. Do you agree with that? I understand that yesterday you did not fully do your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. That is how it will be. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is it agreeable to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: In principle, in principle, we don't object, but it depends upon the questions the counsel will put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. He will try to avoid any leading questions. You may move on, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Mandelbaum: In those cases when you helped detained Muslims to leave the Heliodrom, who did you go to? Full name.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I went to Berko Pusic, and when he didn't do it within two days, I went to Mr. Slobodan Bozic, who got his jeep ready and brought two of his colleagues along, and I believe one had his wife with him. I said exactly whom I wanted to get out, and they went into the Heliodrom, looked for them, and brought them to Mostar. It was sometime around the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It wasn't clear yesterday whether during the conflict between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croat defence council, that is, following the 9th of May, 1993, whether you ever met Mr. Vinko Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. After the 9th of May, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. That is all I wanted to ask you. Mr. Mandelbaum, did we get your meaning wrong yesterday, or was there a misunderstanding? Because to me it was perfectly clear. But for the record, to make it as comprehensible as possible, you said that assuming that a friend, a Muslim friend of yours was taken from the Heliodrom to work in Vinko Martinovic, Stela's, unit, that only then you would have gone to Vinko Martinovic and asked him about that person. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you did not understand me well, sir. I said: Had a Jew been taken away, and I tried with the legal authorities, that is, the HVO, the military police, to inquire about his fate, if he wouldn't be detained by them, then I would go around the town inquiring about him, and thus would I get to Stela and ask him whether perhaps he was with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mandelbaum, I said a moment ago that you're a very valuable and there are very few persons in Mostar, who during the conflict between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croat Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Defence Council, after the 9th of May, 1993, went to all the political and military institutions of Herceg-Bosna and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is it true that you never came across our client Vinko Martinovic, that he was just a foot soldier on the front line, and that therefore you had no reason to look him out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's a leading question, there's no doubt about it. You are leading the witness deliberately. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I must join you in your objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you should not answer this question, because this Trial Chamber does not allow the Defence counsel to ask you this question. You have to understand. Or you may put it another way or try to rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wanted to avoid any possible misunderstanding, because that was the case yesterday, and that is why I took the liberty of asking such a question, and I stand by it. But I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandelbaum, do you have any direct knowledge whether Vinko Martinovic was in any of these institutions or organisations that you visited in order to be able to move around Mostar freely, to gain access to the Heliodrom and the like?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's again a leading question, though rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, I think somehow the witness has answered your question. Well, you may ask, you know, what the witness knows about the role Mr. Vinko Martinovic played.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I shall repeat the question in this way: In view of the role that you played, and you said a moment ago that you did not come across Vinko Martinovic, what was he, in your eyes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my eyes, he was a legend living in the town and whose name many people used to brag about. Stela told me this, Stela told me to take a flat, Stela told me so and Stela told me so. And the job he did, what he did, I do not know that, and I said already that Stela was not in any of these institutions, because these were all civilian institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mandelbaum, I believe you will agree with me when I say that there's always one rotten apple on every tree which must be removed in order to save the crop.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... who put in question is leading. I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Seric. It is really a leading question. I don't think, you know, by asking this question will do your case any good. We understand your intention. You should not ask this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this wasn't a question. This is something which is a notorious fact and which needs no proof. But it is notorious that there are rotten fruit on every tree. Now I'm moving on to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I know, but you are not allowed to make a statement. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, when you mentioned and said that two or three soldiers were arrogant, were you referring to those people or to the whole unit, or Vinko Martinovic in person?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: The statement is a wrong interpretation of the testimony, yesterday's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think so. I remember that the witness said some soldiers are very arrogant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: But not two or three soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let me hear what the witness is going to tell us. Witness, you may answer that question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I said that those guys threw their weight about. They had big cars, with their brakes screeching, they brandished their weapons, and I still see those guys in Mostar, in some coffee bars there, and they still throw their weight about but do not carry any weapons any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandelbaum, thank you very much. Thank you for coming to give your testimony before this Court and helping to establish the real truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, do you have any cross-examination considering of the new elements you feel that have come up during the re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour. I only have one question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, did you have any contacts with the Defence last night?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not speak with them last night. Last night, after this, I went to see a friend of mine in Leiden and returned only at half past 11.00. When I returned from the Court, I went into the hotel. They were sitting there with other witnesses, but I never even approached them. I didn't even have my dinner in the hotel. I went straight away -- I went straight away to Leiden with this friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Who do you mean "they" with sitting with other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: These three counsel: Mr. Seric, the gentleman in the middle, and a young lawyer. The three of them were sitting with four witnesses who had arrived from Mostar to testify, and they were sitting in the hotel lobby. That is, I was with those witnesses too when they arrived, but this Dutch lady who recorded this film, and I wanted you to see it in order to get a better picture of Mostar, she came and I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not exchange with them a single word, or with any of those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from the Judges? Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Mandelbaum, can I ask you a question about Mostar before these terrible events? If we take the period before the 1st inter-party elections, was there any racial or ethnic or inter-religious friction in the town?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mere fact that I don't have an uncle, I don't have a grandfather, that I don't have other relatives, that I married a Croat, and so did my brother, speaks for itself, and I hope that after this war the situation will be the same. I never could believe that the war could happen. So my wife is a Croat, and I have four children. And to answer your question, there were no frictions amongst members of different religions. The only thing that did exist in Mostar was that in one part of West Mostar, Croats built their houses, and in east Mostar, Serbs built their houses in one part. And there was a third part of the town where they built houses together. And in the town, people lived together, in high-rise buildings, they socialised. My best man was a Serb, if that means anything to you. So we all lived together. We had an ideal life, and I would wish it upon my child to have the youth that I had when I was young. We had the feeling of safety and mutual understanding. I really had a good youth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Is there any even glimmer of that kind of life returning to Mostar, or is it all gone?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: For as long as Nazi fascist parties are in power and there are Nazi parties which spread insecurity among the people, I don't think that peace will be restored in Mostar. I believe if SFOR was to withdraw from Mostar, the war would break out in 24 hours, for a simple reason: The things for which the war started in the first place are still in place. There are still things unfinished. And I believe that the division of territory was the main reason for the war, and I'm sorry that I had to answer in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You are not the first one to say that, so don't worry. Can I ask you something about the town during the breakout of hostilities between the ABiH and the HVO? Could people move around freely in the town, or were there curfews and police stops and showing of ID, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell you about Mostar, because I spent the entire war in Mostar. I didn't go to any other towns in Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the 9th of May, when the Muslims started being persecuted from Mostar, Muslims found it very hard to accept. As I told you yesterday, Muslims and Croats never waged a war before that. They were always allies. In the first war, in the Second World War. And that is why they saw the 9th of May as a treason. At that time, there was a curfew. I don't know when was that. I believe it was 8.00 in the afternoon [as interpreted]. There was a curfew, and people couldn't move freely after that. In the streets of Mostar, I don't know whether anybody asked for my ID. I can't remember. But since Mostar is a small town, people mostly lived in buildings, and each building had a so-called commissioner, so that any given moment in time people knew who lived in the building and what was their national or ethnic background. However, during the war, I believe that in Mostar there were a couple of thousands of Muslims who were not expelled. Some of them joined a Muslim-Bosniak organisation, MBO, and a number of Muslims from the Heliodrom were able to leave the Heliodrom by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. addressing this Muslim-Bosniak organisation. I believe that it was this organisation that set them free. So that will be my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. The next question that I want to ask you about is something that I suppose you would have very personal knowledge of from being a Jew who survived the Second World War. Did you get the impression that the expulsions you were talking about were organised, on foot of military orders or political policy, or were they will expulsions which were carried out as personal acts of vindictiveness and hatred? So do you see the distinction? Were they organised expulsions or private people carrying out their own little vendettas?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina, I can say that wherever somebody was a minority, they were expelled. In Mostar, the expulsion was for political reasons. There were two regions. In one of them, Croats would be a majority. I believe that this was misunderstood. It was a misconception, and on that foot the persecution started, but the perpetrators are a different story. As far as the personal vendetta and the hatred amongst the people, amongst Catholics and Muslims, I can tell you that this didn't exist. There were very few people who did not get along for some previous reasons, but this was certainly not because of a religious bias.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understand what you were saying very well, Mr. Mandelbaum. You were saying that the persecution of the Muslims or the expulsion of the Muslims was politically motivated. But in relation to Mostar, we've heard the evidence of a number of people who were forcibly expelled. They've given their evidence. Do you know anything about these expulsions, individual expulsions? Were they organised by the army from orders or by small groups of people acting on their own? Your answer wasn't clear in relation to that. You may not know, but if you -- from your experience.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Based on my experience, I believe that these small groups persecuted Muslims to a small extent, to plunder, to loot, and for that reason. The expulsion of Muslims from the city of Mostar started on the 20th of April, and later on it repeated on the 9th of May, and it was a political decision of the then leadership, in order to create an ethnically clean Mostar, for Mostar to become the capital of Herceg-Bosna. In the town in which there were 34 per cent Muslims and 33 per cent Croats before the war, Mostar couldn't be the capital. I believe that it was a political decision, and then this was implemented by the military units of the HVO. So people who expelled Muslims were mostly not from Mostar. These people came from Citluk, from Listica, from Bosnia, and it was done by these people. I told you that we knew each other very well in Mostar, if not by name, but at least we know each other from sight. And I believe that the units who did -- perpetrated all these things, they had an order from Grude as to what should be done, what should be carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You can't imagine how helpful your evidence has been to me personally, Mr. Mandelbaum. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge's questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've got a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Mandelbaum, in response to Your Honour's question about the curfew, you said that such a situation existed in Mostar after the 9th of May, and who imposed that curfew?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: The curfew was introduced by the mayor of Mostar and the town administration, his town administration. It was announced on the radio that as of then there would be a curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And was this curfew valid in respect of the whole population of Mostar or only in respect of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: The curfew was imposed on everybody but those who war uniforms and who patrolled the city and did whatever they were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And my next question will be in response to Her Honour's questions, you also said that it were not people from Mostar who were expelling Muslims, but people from Listica and Grude. Do you mean Listica, Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, Mr. Seric. Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness never mentioned people from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. No. The question is not asking about the people from Mostar. Witness, you may answer that question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the expulsion of Muslims in 1993 was carried out by the HVO members who were not from Mostar, who were from Siroki Brijeg or Listica - it is the same town - from Citluk, from Grude, and from other parts of Bosnia. You have to understand that it was the refugees who were the fiercest fighters, that the refugees fought on both sides, on the Muslim side and on the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Just continuing my question about Siroki Brijeg. Do you know of any particular unit which was involved, I mean unit from Siroki Brijeg, which was involved in the expulsion of Muslims from Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this question has not been raised either on direct or on cross-examination, or by the Judges, so I don't know where this re-direct, re-examination and the new cross-examination is leading to. I cannot allow that -- I cannot agree that everything can be allowed, and especially if something has not been raised so far, that it can be raised now at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in the answer of the questions, the witness said that those people from Listica and the Siroki Brijeg, so naturally the following question is to ask which unit, whether this witness knows, those people are from. This question is allowed. Witness, you may answer this question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which unit it was. They did not have any insignia that would give the name of the unit. However, I came across people in Mostar who spoke a different dialect, which was not the dialect of Mostar. And when I told you that these were units from Listica or from Siroki Brijeg, then from Grude, Citluk, and from Bosnia, I said that these people were those who came to Mostar from somewhere else, to expel Muslims from Mostar, and that was done for the reason for the people not to know who were the ones who had expelled them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Why? I'll allow you to ask a question which is related to your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any questions related to my client, but I have questions related to the indictment and to -- related to the questions asked by Her Honour Clark. That could be related to my client, and that one question would be whether the witness knows what was the destiny of Croats on the east side and what happened with them? Were they expelled? The gentleman is a humanitarian work, and maybe he could tell us whether Croats were expelled from Mostar as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, is this question related to Judge Clark's question? Is this question related to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, we don't think so. You are not allowed to ask this question. You have to understand. We know that all the people, no matter what ethnicity, what nationalities, during that period suffered a lot, but we have to concentrate on the scope of the indictment and the questions asked by the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with due respect, here we are talking about the town of Mostar, and Judge Clark's questions were relative to the town of Mostar. The witness was talking about Mostar. Your Honour Clark, you are interested in the destiny of all the people in Mostar and so are we. That's how the witnesses testify here, and that's how we have understood him here. So my question is a follow-up, because I have understood the role of this witness as somebody who would be talking about the destiny of the entire population of the town of Mostar, of all the people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, you can take it that we know that not only the Muslim population suffered during the war. We know that. There's no dispute about that. And you see, we have to follow the Rules. This is not your witness, so how can you re-examine unless specifically your client's position has been negatively altered or he's been prejudiced in any way? You can take it for granted that we now know that Serbs, Jews, Yugoslavs, Muslims, and Croats suffered horribly during the war, but the issue we're dealing with, as Judge Liu has pointed out to you, is the indictment, and we have to have some order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to give your evidence. We appreciate your testimony very much, and the usher will show you out of the room, and we all wish you a good journey back home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wish you would have had the time to look at this video footage that was delivered to you two years ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any documents to tender? Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, no documents to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got one exhibit to tender, Exhibit P796.3. This is ECMM report read out yesterday in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, I don't think this document is translated into the B/C/S. Although we use the interpretation here during the trial, but to be fair, this document has to be translated into the B/C/S so that the two accused could not be in the adverse, disadvantaged position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will take into consideration of the admission of that document when we receive the translation of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: By all means, we'll have it translated and submit it to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the witness, please. And there are some protective measures for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Have you hurt your back? You don't look well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm very ill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You're ill?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes. But still, I cannot let the lady work alone. I would like to help you, if you need help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Very briefly, if I could use the time. Sorry, the witness is just now -- I was just reminded that we had requested the other day the c.v. or curriculum vitae of the expert of Davor Marijan. We still have not received that, because I realise that we may finish this witness today and not be in session again until next week. We're still seeking that c.v., Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think this morning I received a c.v. Maybe Mr. Par could clarify this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, we received a c.v., but unfortunately it was not for the witness we sought. It was for another witness but not for Mr. Marijan, which we still do not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we said we would send the c.v. We have received it. It is being translated. We hope that the translation will be completed by the end of the day, and then we will send it to the Prosecution. You have received another c.v., the c.v. of our other expert doctor, so our obligation still stands, and we will comply with it. But the Prosecution knows everything about the expert, because he cooperated with them in the past. So we are not hiding anything from them. This is our obligation, we are aware of it, and we will comply with it, maybe even by the end of the day today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Par, your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Before we start, I would like to inform you that you have been granted protection measures for your testimony, and that is the protection of your face and name. So your identity will not be known, and parts of this session which could reveal your identity will be given in the so-called closed session. Can you please look at the piece of paper with your name on it. If this is indeed your name, just say yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You mean private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us, in only so many words, whether you were militarily engaged during the Serb aggression, and if yes, where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: I was, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us what unit, where? Wait. Just wait.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: The command of the military district of Mostar, which is in the former Lesnina building, Lesnina building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: The 9th of May, 1993, the day when the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims started, where were you then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: On the 9th of May I was at home, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And when did you report to your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: I reported in the morning, at the headquarters, when I was due.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Which is the 10th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: The 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell us: In 1993, in this conflict between the Croats and the Muslims, were you always with that unit or did you perhaps go to join some other units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: I was at the command of the military district in Mostar all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Will you tell us whether at that time, that is, in 1993, the Croat-Muslim war, did you communicate with Vinko Martinovic, Stela?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you, within the framework of your jobs and duties, communicate with units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you, during that same time, ever go to the separation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you ever participate personally in some military operations with a rifle or something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you know an individual called Nenad Haramandic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us: How did you know him? What can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: I knew Nenad Haramandic through my late father. They were friends. They patronised together, two or three taverns in Mostar. Apart from that, I did not socialise with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please: Did you know members of his family: His wife, his son?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you ever visit their house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Will you tell me if you used to see Nenad Haramandic during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you know that Nenad Haramandic was detained at the Heliodrom camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: During the war, or after it, did you learn anything about Nenad Haramandic's fate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you, during the war, used to see Nenad Haramandic's wife? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you perhaps see Nenad Haramandic's son sometime in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What about after the war? Did then you see Nenad Haramandic's wife or son?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so, Your Honour. We're coming to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So my last question was --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: During the war, whether I used to see the wife or son of Nenad Haramandic's. That was the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you in any way discuss Nenad Haramandic's fate with any member of his family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you know an individual called Kladusak from Jablanica, who, in 1993, was a prisoner of war in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we go into private session, please, for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have very few questions for the witness, but I think it's best to be in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Witness, in the town of Mostar, have you heard of or do you know people who have a different nickname from you, a nickname Cica, C-i-c-a?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from Judges? Well, thank you very much, Witness, for coming here to give your evidence. When the usher pulls down the blinds, she will show you out of the room. We all wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Witness, just wait a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, Mr. President, there was one very brief issue we wanted to raise with the Trial Chamber concerning next week's proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll wait until the witness leaves the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, one of the expert witnesses scheduled for next week to testify in open session is a Dr. Begic, and we among ourselves on the Prosecution bench have a bit of a concern. We have read the expert submissions of Mr. Begic and know that he will be commenting on the testimony of another person who has testified in this case in open session, but he's going to be describing alleged competencies of this other witness, alleged mental disorders, things of that nature, and then commenting on that witness's ability to recall, I suppose, and to give reliable testimony. The only concern we had was whether that sort of testimony, where one person is commenting on deficiencies, mental deficiencies of another person who has appeared is something that could perhaps be dealt more appropriately in a private or a closed session, so that, as a form of protection of the person who testified previously in this case, and that is a bit of a concern we have out of fairness for the previous witness, whether it's really appropriate for us to be talking about his sanity or lack thereof in open proceedings here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any response, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course I want to respond. This is a witness, or rather, an expert witness, for the Defence. What my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. learned friend has just said, he absolutely objects to what that witness himself asked for when his protective measures were raised. He requested that he testify in open session, and in that open session, he said that he had received psychiatric treatment and that he had a certain mental complaints. And after him, we heard a number of witnesses who confirmed that, again in open sessions. So whom do we protect now when we hear an expert witness about this? The diagnosis, just a diagnostic paper issued by the hospital in Mostar. When the witness himself did not want it. I do not know what the Prosecutor wants, that the public does not learn what quality of testimonies -- of his testimony was. I mean, he's our witness and we are requesting an open session. We do not want -- we do not need any protective measures for our expert witness, and I must vehemently object to this Prosecution's proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, I don't think you get the meaning of what the Prosecution said. I think the purpose of his concern is to protect the personal privacy of the witness, if I may say like this. As I understand, in many jurisdictions, the personal history of an illness or diagnosis rendered by a doctor are quite different from the comments made by some ordinary people. This is touched upon the very privacy of a person. I think we have to respect the privacy of all the people before this courtroom. My suggestion is: We'll start the trial, the hearing, in open session, and when we come to the specific aspect, both parties are free to raise to the attention of this Trial Chamber to move to the private session. Is that agreeable to both parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not agreeable to me, Mr. President, because the witness himself has refused such protection. In his testimony, he himself, and he even pronounced his diagnosis aloud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, I still think that you don't understand the meaning of the request from the Prosecution. At this stage, if you do not agree with this suggestion, I'm afraid we have to make a ruling that we'll start with that witness in open session, and both parties are free to request to come into the private session whenever they believe it's necessary. So decided. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if you have finished this subject. I'd like to raise something else that has to do with my last witness, the expert witness, Professor Ancic. I don't know if it is possible. I don't know if the previous witness has been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wanted to ask you the following: Our last expert witness, Professor Ancic - this is our joint witness - was scheduled to appear as our last witness, and over the phone he told me that he had some previous commitments and that he cannot be here before the 18th or the 19th of September, which is Friday. So I wanted to ask you to agree with my proposal that we hear this witness on the 23rd, which is a Monday, when it is sure that the witness can actually be here. This is all that I have to ask of you, Your Honours, and of my learned friends on the Prosecution bench. According to our previous schedule, I thought that my colleagues will finish around the 20th, and that is how I scheduled my witness, who, however, has some commitments, commitments related to his university duties. That's why I wanted to ask you to allow me to call this witness on the 23rd, which is a Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the information. On our part, there is no problem at all. We have to check with the registrar to see a suitable courtroom is arranged for the hearing. But it is really our desire to hear the witnesses one after another rather than stop for a few days, then have another witness. But since you have the difficulty in calling your witness, I think this Trial Chamber will do its utmost to accommodate your request. Mr. Seric, is it possible for us to hear the witnesses next week this Friday? I was told that they are going to arrive here this Friday and we will have afternoon session. I just ask you whether there is a possibility for us to hear the witness on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witnesses arrive by plane from Sarajevo via Zurich and they will arrive in the hotel around 10.00 in the evening on the 13th of September, that is, on Friday, around 10.00 in the evening. Therefore, it is not going to be possible to hear them on Friday. The first day after that that we can hear them is Monday, the 16th of September. We have envisaged to finish two witnesses on the 16th, and the next witness, the expert, could be finished on the 17th. That is, my direct examination could be finished on the 17th, and this would bring our part of the case to an end. So it can be envisaged that our direct examination of all our witnesses will be finished on the 17th, and then it will depend on the Prosecution how long they will take to cross-examine. And maybe just a suggestion, and I'm sorry for taking this liberty. If you will decide to hear my colleague Krsnik's witness on the 23rd, that we should maybe have a break on Monday and Tuesday, and that we start working then and conclude our work on the 23rd. So prolong this break that we are going to have now, and instead of working on Monday and Tuesday, we should then start working on Wednesday and continue until my colleague Krsnik's witness is finished. And I apologise for this suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I did not get you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just heard your suggestion that we should work continuously. With regard to the fact that we will need two days for three witnesses, maybe these two days should start on the 18th, that the break would be on the 16th, and on the 17th, that would bring us closer to the 23rd if you grant Mr. Krsnik's witness to be heard on 23rd, which is Monday. We are prepared to do that. But obviously it will be as you decide. That is to avoid another break after our three witnesses before Mr. Krsnik's witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, there's a problem that your witness will stay in The Hague too long. I don't think that the registrar will agree with this suggestion, even if we made a decision on this respect. So we have to stick to our original arrangement, to hear the witness next Monday. And since that both parties have plenty of time in this week and the next week, my suggestion is that you might, thinking of the final briefs, and report to any rejoinder witnesses. We have already made a decision that we'll break before the 4th of October so that both parties will have plenty time to submit and prepare their final brief, as well as prepare their witnesses, in rebuttal and rejoinder procedures. Here I have to suggest that this Trial Chamber adopted a very strict view concerning with the witnesses of the rebuttal and the rejoinder procedures. We will not accept new elements in those procedures. We only hope those parties could call the witness directly related to the evidence raised in your cases or in the other party's cases. It's not a procedure for the retrial. Having said that, we will rise until next Monday afternoon in courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: To be reconvened on Monday, the 16th day of September 2002, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.23 p.m.
